new_statements.quote: According to Aze (1971: 35), in Gorum isolated words, that is, those produced in isolation or not embedded within a larger prosodic structure, stress is generally found in word-final position, if the final syllable is closed; otherwise, primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable in Gorum nominal forms. Gorum verb forms exhibit a range of morpholexical complications that deviate from this idealized system.
new_statements.citation: Anderson, Gregory D. S. & Felix Rau. 2008. Gorum. In Gregory D. S. Anderson (ed.), The Munda Languages, 381-433. London/New York: Routledge. Stress subsection (the one preceding '2.6 Morphophonology'), p. 386 — reporting Aze, F. Richard. 1971. Parengi (Gorum) phonemic summary, mimeo, Deccan College & SIL, p. 35.
new_statements.locator: p. 386, stress subsection of section 2 (Phonology), immediately before '2.6 Morphophonology'; Google Books volume 6GzxBwAAQBAJ page id PA386
new_statements.rule_in_words: In citation-form (isolated) words, stress falls on the final syllable when that syllable is closed (CVC); when the final syllable is open, primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable — stated for nominal forms. Verb forms do not follow this cleanly because of morphological complexity. The reported pattern is thus a final-syllable-weight rule (heavy final attracts stress, otherwise penult), not a fixed position.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; a search-within-volume query for "secondary stress" co-occurring with Gorum returns 0 hits in The Munda Languages.
new_statements.exceptions: 'Gorum verb forms exhibit a range of morpholexical complications that deviate from this idealized system.' The rule is hedged ('generally'). Hock & Bashir 2016 (snippet) add the second-hand caution that such Munda judgments (citing Aze 1971: 35 for Gorum) may rest on two- or three-syllable words only.
new_statements.domain_note: Explicitly restricted to 'isolated words, that is, those produced in isolation or not embedded within a larger prosodic structure' (citation forms), and the penult default is stated for nominal forms; verb forms are said to deviate. Nothing said about phrase-level stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Gorum = Parengi = Parenga (Glottolog pare1266, ISO pcj); Anderson & Rau 2008 describe 'Gorum' and Aze's 1969-72 data come from Bhejaguda village, Koraput District, Odisha (Aze 1973: 235). No dialect split is at issue. Not to be confused with the Dravidian 'Parji'/'Parenga Parja' or with Gadaba (Gutob), both listed among the alternate names.
